record.statement: If finite graphs G_n converge locally weakly to a nonamenable transitive graph G, is the local limit of the FK(p,q) random-cluster measures on G_n (especially q > 1) the wired measure on G? Known for the WUSF (q = p = 0) and for Ising on regular trees (Montanari-Mossel-Sly: symmetric mixture of plus and minus).
record.title: Local limits of random-cluster models converging to nonamenable transitive graphs are wired

record.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
record.key_identity: Finite-graph complement of a ball connected in the percolation configuration <=> wired boundary condition in the limit.
record.method: Separate the random-cluster question from its spin-model consequence.
record.obstruction: Giant uniqueness for non-transitive local approximants.
record.result: For q = 2 the Montanari-Mossel-Sly result is about the ISING local limit on regular trees, which is the symmetric mixture of the plus and minus extremal measures; in random-cluster language this corresponds to the wired measure (the mixture of the two spin phases is the Edwards-Sokal image of the wired FK measure). So the q = 2, tree case is consistent with the question. For general q > 1 and a general nonamenable limit, a route: the finite-volume random-cluster measure on G_n is sandwiched (for q >= 1) between free and wired measures on any finite ball by monotonicity, and the local limit is sandwiched between the free and wired limits on G; the question is whether the limit hits the wired end. Wired is favoured because finite graphs have no 'boundary' (a ball's complement in G_n is connected and large), which acts like wired boundary conditions provided the complement percolates, i.e. for p above the threshold where the free and wired measures differ the finite graph's complement of a ball is itself supercritical and connected, wiring the boundary. For p below that threshold free = wired and the question is empty. So for q >= 1 the answer is yes whenever the complement of a ball in G_n is connected within the percolation configuration with high probability, which is a uniqueness-of-the-giant statement on G_n (C0141-type, proved for transitive G_n by Easo-Hutchcroft); for non-transitive G_n it is exactly the open part. Reduction: for transitive G_n and q >= 1 the answer should be yes via giant uniqueness; general G_n open.
